To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the presence of a single strain of microorganism in the intestine is sufficient to stimulate the immune system and produce antibodies.

the germfree animal has a decreased level of serum gamma globulin, and that the addition of a single strain of bacteria to the germfree animal results in a rise of alphaz and beta globulin, but no rise in gamma globulin, for the first two weeks post contamination.

the presence of an intact immune system is essential to the health and welfare of the individual, and that the absence of a normal microbiome is not sufficient to explain the health and welfare status of an animal.
In summary, our research is concerned with
studies on the immunological response of germfree animals to antigens.
the effects of a single strain of bacteria, E. coli, on the serum protein and antibody levels in rats.
the study of the effects of various microorganisms on the host.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
germfree animals are not immunologically deficient, but rather that their immune responses are altered in certain respects.

the germfree animal, in general, is characterized by a hypogammag lobulinemia and that the normal flora, at least in part, contributes to the maintenance of normal levels of the various serum protein fractions.
the germfree-reared animals are hypogammaglo-buline~nica and the monocontaminated animals are hyper-gammaglobulinemic.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the serum protein fractions of the germfree animal are lower than those of conventional animals, that the germfree animal has fewer antibacterial agglutinin antibodies than the monocontaminated and conventional animal, that these antibodies are not species specific and that they are formed in response to dietary antigens.
the germfree animal is not as different from its conventional counterpart as is often believed.

the serum protein fractions in germfree animals, in the absence of an associated microbial population, are at lower levels than those found in conventional animals and that the levels in monocontaminated animals are intermediate between those found in germfree and conventional animals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need to be very careful about how we interpret the results of these kinds of studies.
the germfree rat is a useful animal in which to study the immune response to a purified protein antigen.
we need a new approach to understanding the relationship between the gut microbiota and disease.
